title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, fully archived paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) that tested whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic validator). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) producing model_calls_used = 200. Observed (confirmatory set): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that the deterministic verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration, and exploratory ROC reserves) for informative repeats.

sections.introduction:
Automating human‑intent → device‑configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) is a growing NetOps research area because it can reduce operator effort and speed maintenance workflows. Incorrectly sequenced or otherwise unsafe configuration changes can cause outages, security exposures, or policy violations; therefore, multiple works advocate pairing LLM generators with deterministic validators or sandboxed simulators in generate–validate–repair pipelines to reduce operational risk (e.g., Bilal et al., 2026; Ferrag et al., 2026).

We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) to answer a focused causal question: How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic validator → optional repair) change the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals produced by a hosted LLM under preregistered benign and adversarial prompt clusters? The preregistered estimand was the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded minus baseline) computed by an exact McNemar two‑sided test with paired bootstrap confidence intervals (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Key preregistered design features were N=200 paired tasks, deterministic task generation and seeding, explicit exclusion/missingness rules, and a reserved exploratory calibration budget. The executed run used shared_initial_candidate semantics to conserve model calls; this choice and the observed outcomes make the confirmatory estimand non‑informative for the selected model and task set. The manuscript therefore reports (1) the preregistered, deterministic run (archived); (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the run was non‑informative for the preregistered causal hypothesis; and (3) concrete, artifact‑supported design recommendations for informative repeats.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and prototype reports document rapid interest in LLMs for NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, limited remediation), and they emphasize both potential and safety concerns (Bilal et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2024). Tool‑augmentation—pairing LLMs with deterministic validators/simulators or constrained executors—is a recurring architecture shown to reduce explicit constraint violations on curated tasks when the verifier faithfully encodes domain constraints (Zhang et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026). Work on guardrails and schema‑based interfaces highlights operational trade‑offs: stricter deterministic checks can lower unsafe acceptances but may increase false refusals and operator burden unless evaluated with ROC‑style diagnostics and adversarial stress tests (Tarun Yadav, 2026; Ando, 2026).

Methodological literature argues for workflow‑centred, replayable, and sandboxed evaluations that include deterministic generators, explicit initial/final states, and archived validator traces; such protocols improve reproducibility and enable diagnostic ROC and failure‑mode analysis (Ferrag et al., 2026; Bilal et al., 2026). Our study aligns with these recommendations by preregistering a paired causal estimand, using deterministic synthetic tasks with explicit required sequences, and archiving full validator traces and execution manifests for deterministic replay.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered as cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on binary SAFE indicators from a deterministic sandbox validator. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar; CI: paired bootstrap percentile (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). N=200 paired tasks were chosen to power detection of an approximate 7 percentage‑point paired reduction assuming baseline unsafe ≈10–15%.

Task generator and scope. A deterministic generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks covering single‑AS multi‑device topologies and a constrained field set {admin, mtu, vlan}. Each task included initial_state, expected_final_state, an explicit required_sequence, and difficulty metadata. Adversarial prompts were constructed from a preregistered obfuscation template set intended to increase baseline unsafe frequency.

Compared pipelines. Baseline: accept the LLM candidate and perform post hoc scoring with deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Guarded: validate the same LLM candidate in a deterministic sandboxed validator; repairs were permitted by design but were not invoked in confirmatory episodes (repair traces are null in scoring JSONs). Because repairs were not applied, the guarded arm implements validation only in the confirmatory set.

Generation semantics, budgeting, and execution contract. The preregistration allowed two generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation (two independent LLM draws per task) or shared_initial_candidate (one LLM draw per task scored by both arms). To conserve hosted model budget the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation=false). The preregistered independent per‑arm budget would have required ~400 model calls; the executed shared run consumed model_calls_used = 200. Analysis and reconciliation artifacts certify exactly these counts and the absence of technical failures.

Scoring and analysis. Deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned validator.valid (1=SAFE, 0=UNSAFE) plus structured violation lists. Confirmatory binary outcomes derive from validator.valid. Analysis was performed by paired_binary_analysis_v1, producing the 2×2 contingency (n11,n10,n01,n00), exact McNemar p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Missingness/exclusion rules (single automatic retry, deterministic duplicate detection, nondeterminism flags) were applied per preregistration; no confirmatory pairs were excluded.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and provider audit. The execution manifest reports completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200. Provider audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and cache_miss_count = 200; deterministic reconciliation checks passed and no contamination flags were raised.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. The deterministic validator labeled every confirmatory episode SAFE: baseline SAFE successes = 200/200; guarded SAFE successes = 200/200. The paired contingency counts are n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. From these counts the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000; seed = 1729). These numerical outputs are identical to archived analysis artifacts (condition_summary.csv and paired_contingency_table.csv).

Representative traces and repair status. Representative scoring JSONs show identical shared_initial_candidate content across baseline and guarded episodes and validator traces with violation_count = 0 and valid = true for every confirmatory item. repair_provider_trace fields are null in all confirmatory scoring JSONs, confirming that no automatic repairs were invoked; consequently the guarded arm performed validation only and did not generate distinct candidate proposals in confirmatory episodes.

Missingness, contamination, exploratory reserves. The run consumed only the confirmatory budget; the preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks for ROC/refusal calibration) was not used prior to confirmatory execution. Missingness_summary records complete_pairs = 200 with zero failed or unscorable episodes, and contamination_summary contains no flags.
sections.discussion:
Diagnostic synthesis. The degenerate contingency (n11=200, n10=n01=n00=0) arises from three archived facts: (1) the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics produced a single LLM candidate per task that both arms scored; (2) deterministic_netops_validator_v5 labeled every such candidate as valid; and (3) no repairs were applied in confirmatory episodes. With identical per‑pair candidates and identical validator decisions, the paired contrast mechanically lacks discordant pairs needed by McNemar’s test, so the preregistered causal estimand could not be evaluated.

Design implications. When the causal question is the effect of adding a verifier to generation, the paired design requires arm‑level variation. Under shared generation semantics, discordance can arise only via repairs applied by the guarded arm or via nondeterministic validators; neither mechanism was present here. If budget permits, independent per‑arm generation is the straightforward way to restore testability (≈+200 model calls for our N=200). Alternatively, include preregistered deterministic repairs that will reliably produce altered guarded candidates and archive repair traces for analysis.

Artifact‑grounded recommendations for informative repeats (all follow from archived manifest and analysis counts): 1) Use independent per‑arm generation for confirmatory paired contrasts unless repairs are consistently applied and archived; 2) reserve and consume the prespecified exploratory calibration budget to tune adversarial transforms until baseline unsafe prevalence meets power assumptions; 3) pilot‑check contingency counts on a small holdout and abort the full confirmatory run if the pilot produces a ceiling/floor outcome; and 4) if independent per‑arm draws are infeasible, change the estimand to a single‑arm absolute unsafe‑rate estimate or to refusal/repair conversion rates (these alternatives were preregistered as secondary/exploratory estimands).

Threats to validity and externality. Internal validity: the critical execution choice (shared_initial_candidate) constrained arm‑level stochasticity and therefore the testability of the paired estimand. Construct validity: synthetic tasks limited fields (admin/mtu/vlan) and task families, so validator completeness versus production failure modes is unknown. External validity: results apply only to the evaluated model (gpt‑5‑mini) and the synthetic task family; no multi‑vendor, multi‑AS, or production deployments were evaluated. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate (~10–15%); that assumption did not hold in execution, invalidating the planned inferential sensitivity.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully archived preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt‑5‑mini baseline generation and a deterministic validator‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for the declared model, both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and the baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis was not testable in this run. The scientific contribution is therefore methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts that permit exact replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration, exploratory ROC estimation, and pilot checks) for informative repeats. Practitioners should align generation semantics and resource budgets with the estimand when designing confirmatory NetOps evaluations involving tool‑augmentation.

Table 1 summarizes the key execution resource trade‑offs and confirmatory counts to help operators plan informative repeats (N, model calls used vs planned, and contingency counts). Representative archived traces and all analysis artifacts are available in the bundled execution and analysis archives for deterministic replay and inspection.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
